bloks.name: STRAIGHT UP
bloks.title: Cold Water
bloks.dek: Your moment in the mirror. Clear, not cynical.

body.text: Cold water is your moment in the mirror, letting accountability do its quiet, self-solving work.
It’s when you realize no “new year goals” worksheet is going to drag you anywhere.

body.cap: Cold water seems harsh until it’s not.
body.alt: “Wow” reaction GIF from The Jim Jefferies Show

body.text: We’ve never had more access to information, yet we can’t agree on the facts.
That makes trust crucial, because people and systems can look one way while something else is happening underneath.
Cold water doesn’t make you cynical. It makes you clear. Then it’s on you to act.

Until one day, it changed.

body.text: You found what you’re looking for. You got the thing you’ve always wanted. The best advice is right in front of you.
“But you keep scrolling.”
This phrase reached its loudest moment on the @mylifeordebt Instagram account.

The meme’s been around, but they turned it into a marketing mainstay: post after post lays out a usable blueprint (money, credit, business), then comes the same closing line: “but you keep scrolling.”

body.alt: A young woman in a park wearing a black T-shirt that reads “but you keep scrolling…”

body.label: 🗺️ Treasure Hunt: what classic meme is this tee design based on? Answer on the Back Page →

body.text: It became the ultimate sales takeaway: the objection gets handled before it can arrive.
Because the problem isn’t always access, or even information.
It’s the dopamine loop of doom-scrolling—and the fear that if you stop, you’ll have to act.
We say we want the answer, but when it finally shows up, we scroll anyway—hoping the next thumb-flick holds something better.

bloks.name: BEHIND THE REEL
bloks.title: “Free Kuminga”
bloks.dek: An AI-generated protest music reel confronting hypocrisy in social justice and the corporatization of pro sports.

body.text: Right under everyone’s noses in San Francisco, a contradiction has been playing out in real time.

Free Kuminga began as a creative response to something that felt deeply off: a young basketball player with visible talent, growth, and crowd support being repeatedly sidelined through abstract language, shifting explanations, and institutional silence, while the media largely echoed those same explanations back to the public.

items.alt: Black T-shirt on a hanger: FREE KUMINGA.
Canvas tote stitched with FREE KUMINGA.

body.text: The reel is exaggerated on purpose. It reflects a feeling many fans share but rarely see articulated: that something unfair has been normalized, and that power is being insulated from scrutiny.

body.cap: Free Kuminga, the reel. Watch on YouTube.
body.alt: Free Kuminga protest reel

body.text: Jonathan Kuminga entered the NBA as the 7th overall pick in 2021 — raw, athletic, and undeniably impactful. From the beginning, the expectation was a long development timeline, and that made sense.
What stopped making sense was how little changed by year five.
When Kuminga plays, the impact is obvious: energy shifts and the crowd responds. Yet his role stays unstable, his leash short, and his integration incomplete.
Explanations follow: “fit,” “lineups,” “matchups.” Language familiar to anyone who’s watched institutions avoid accountability while sounding reasonable.
This is where the conversation moves beyond basketball.

Steve Kerr—the head coach and the person who controls Kuminga’s role—is widely regarded as a moral voice beyond the sport. He’s spoken at the Democratic National Convention and consistently addresses justice and responsibility.
That public identity is relevant, because values mean the most when they’re tested without cameras pointed at a podium.
What Free Kuminga exposes is the gap between advocacy and execution.

This isn’t about labeling intent. It’s about outcomes and double standards: who gets patience and who absorbs consequences. When legit criticism shows up, it gets redirected downward—reframed as “immaturity,” “attitude,” or “personal failure.”
And the crowd feels it: standing ovations, even after Kuminga’s camp requested a trade. If anything, the support got louder. The sense that something doesn’t add up.
The reel doesn’t resolve these tensions, but it does give a name to them.

It asks a simple question: What does real social justice look like when it’s inconvenient, unscripted, and unfolding in front of everyone? When the crowd keeps saying it doesn’t add up, that’s data. You can’t spin that away.
Takeaway: When institutions protect power, storytelling becomes a form of protest. AI tools now move fast enough to bypass gatekeepers.
Tools: MidJourney / CapCut / Suno

bloks.name: CHAIN REACTION
bloks.title: What Is Kaspa? — Classroom Edition
bloks.dek: Same foundation as Bitcoin, minus the speed bottleneck.

body.alt: Kaspa logo

body.text: Last issue we did Kaspa: Playground Edition. This week we step one foot into the classroom.
Kaspa, in Plain Terms
Bitcoin showed the world what was possible. Kaspa asks a simple follow-up: what if you kept the same foundation, but removed the speed bottleneck?
Kaspa sticks with proof-of-work, keeping the foundation intact: decentralization and security. The difference is speed. It’s faster because the network can process more at once.

body.cap: Kaspa, explained.
body.alt: Chat-style explainer: Kaspa is a super-fast playground for digital money; it processes transactions in parallel.

body.text: The mind behind it, Yonatan Sompolinsky, isn’t new to this game. His earlier work on GHOST is cited in Ethereum’s whitepaper.
The strange part isn’t the tech. It’s how few people are paying attention.
For now.

bloks.name: MUSIC FLOW
bloks.title: Soap&Skin — “Me and the Devil”
bloks.dek: The case for a different read of the Robert Johnson cover.

body.text: The Case for a Different Read

body.cap: Anja Plaschg of Soap&Skin, and Robert Johnson.

body.text: There’s a good chance you’ve heard this song without realizing it. On Instagram and TikTok it shows up as an emotional shortcut: dread, doom, that “something’s wrong in the air” feeling. And yes, it’s haunting. But the online framing tends to flatten it into one default read: selling your soul, surrendering to darkness.
Background note: the original “Me and the Devil Blues” was recorded in 1937 and released in 1938. Soap&Skin’s version came out in 2013 on the Sugarbread EP.

What Soap&Skin does to it is surgical. She drains the song of swing and momentum and leaves slow footsteps, empty space, and a voice that feels like it’s cutting through an abandoned building. That’s why it works so well as “viral bed music.” It builds atmosphere in seconds.
But I hear something else in it.
Most people latch onto the opening like a confession (“Hello Satan… it’s time to go”) and stop there. What if it isn’t surrender, but a decision to face the thing head-on?

links.text: Hello Satan… it’s time to go

body.text: “Me and the devil walkin’ side by side” can read like resignation. It can also read like someone who’s done running. Not “the devil owns me.” More like: fine. Walk with me. I’m looking straight at you.

Then the lyric that feels easiest to miss: “that old evil spirit.” Old. Not new. Not destiny. Not identity. Something lodged deep. Maybe inherited, maybe learned, maybe absorbed. But still something you can name, and maybe something you’re trying to get rid of.

And the ending? People hear the burial lines and assume defeat. I hear a harsher kind of clarity: letting the body take the hit so the “old evil spirit” can finally be sent away. Put on a bus, out of town, done. Exile the thing that’s been riding with you.

This reading fits Soap&Skin as a creator too. When she talks about pain, death, nature, fearlessness, it doesn’t land like a costume. It lands like a lived orientation. The cover ends up feeling less like “devil worship” and more like staring into the dark without blinking.
Not surrender, but a stare-down.
That’s the version of this song I can’t unhear: not surrender, but a stare-down.
Press play. Judge for yourself.
